A flaky test is useful only when the failure leaves enough evidence to classify it.
In my Playwright work, stability comes from three layers: user-facing locators, controlled test data, and API or trace evidence behind the UI result. That makes it possible to separate an application defect from timing, authentication, environment, or test-code problems before anyone reaches for rerun.
A test suite should reduce debugging time, not create another system to debug.
#Playwright #QualityEngineering #TestAutomation #SoftwareTesting

I’ve learned to treat flaky tests as a signal, not just an annoyance.

A test that fails intermittently may be exposing timing assumptions, shared state, unstable data, or a real race condition. Rerunning it until it passes hides the risk and weakens trust in the suite.

The better question is: what changed between the passing and failing runs?

I’m curious where others draw the line between quarantine and investigation. Push back if your approach differs.

A test fails. You rerun it and it passes. Was there a defect? Was the test updated incorrectly? Or did the result change for no apparent reason?

That last case is flakiness: an automated test producing inconsistent results across executions on the same build, environment and inputs.

The issue is not one occasional false failure. When pass rates oscillate, every failure must be triaged twice: first to establish whether it is real, then to fix it if it is. The suite becomes harder to trust and harder to read.

Read the blog to understand why flaky tests are a strategic problem, not just a tactical annoyance: https://lnkd.in/es8uGkjC

#TestAutomation #SoftwareTesting #QualityAssurance

A small rant about flaky tests
 Nothing erodes a team's trust in automation faster than a test suite that cries wolf. Once developers start ignoring red builds because "oh that one's always flaky," your safety net is gone - you just haven't noticed yet. Fixing flaky tests isn't glamorous work, but it's some of the highest-leverage work a QA team can do. Treat flakiness as a bug, not a nuisance.

Most flaky tests aren't flaky.

They're timing bugs wearing a costume.

When a suite "randomly" fails, the easy move is to retry until green. The useful move is to ask: what race did we paper over? What shared state leaked? What assumption about the network died under real traffic?

Retries hide the problem. They don't fix it.

Next time a test flakes twice in a week, treat it like a production incident — not a CI annoyance.

Flaky tests erode trust faster than missing tests do. Once a test suite cries wolf enough times, engineers stop reading the red and start re-running until it goes green. At that point the suite is providing less signal than no suite at all, just more ceremony around ignoring it.

Fixing flakiness is unglamorous work. It rarely gets prioritized on its own, only after someone gets burned by a real bug that a flaky test also happened to be flagging that week.

Treat flaky as a bug in the test, not a fact of life.

#BuildInPublic #SoftwareTesting #QA #TestAutomation

The dangerous part of a flaky test isn't the false failure. It's what happens when teams stop investigating.

Google found that 𝟴𝟰% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀-𝘁𝗼-𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 they observed involved a flaky test.

At Google's scale, 𝟭𝟲% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.

So "probably just flaky" becomes a reasonable assumption - right up until it's wrong.

Nobody ignores a defect on purpose. But when false alarms happen often enough, teams learn to dismiss them.
And eventually, the excuse for a false alarm becomes indistinguishable from the excuse for a real regression.

That's where the risk sits.

If your release process can't distinguish the two, your test suite starts measuring confidence instead of quality.

The next time a test is labelled "𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗸𝘆," ask one question:
Did we prove it was flaky, or did it simply pass the second time?

The tool that made my flaky tests confess: Allure Report. 📊

What sold me isn't the pretty dashboard. It's the history — Allure shows how one test behaved over the last N nightly runs, not just tonight's red or green.

A scenario that "sometimes fails" stops being a mystery when the trend shows it broke the same step 4 of the last 10 runs. That's a flake with a pattern, not bad luck. 🔍

The catch: that trend only exists if you carry the previous results folder between runs. A fresh CI checkout has amnesia — you have to persist history yourself (I keep mine on GitHub Pages).

Do you actually read your test reports, or just check red vs green?

#SDET #TestAutomation #Allure

FlakeyRadar: My Final Year Project 
A few weeks ago I said I'd share more about my final year project; here it is.
FlakeyRadar is a tool I built alongside Gideon Babalola to detect, classify, and automatically repair flaky tests in JavaScript CI pipelines.
Quick context for anyone who hasn't run into this pain: a flaky test is a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails, with no code changes in between. No new bug introduced, but just a non-deterministic test. They quietly kill trust in CI pipelines. Teams start ignoring failed builds because "oh that's probably just flaky," which is a dangerous habit to build.

So for FlakeyRadar, we:
Trained a CodeBERT-based model to classify flaky tests based on 3 flaky test categories (async flaky tests, network-related flaky tests, and concurrency-related flaky tests because these were the flaky tests that occurred the most in the JavaScript environment).
Built a pipeline that plugs into JS CI workflows to detect them automatically
Went a step further with automated repair, not just flagging flaky tests, but attempting to fix them
It became more than just the project we had to submit to graduate. It turned into a genuine research problem we got attached to.

Two month from graduation, and this is one of the things I'm proudest of building. Shoutout to Gideon Babalola for grinding through this with me.
Would love to hear from anyone who has dealt with flaky tests in their own CI pipelines, or anyone working in software testing.  Always up for a conversation.

A bug this week had Microsoft Defender flagging legitimate Google search links as malicious.

Consider what that does to a security product over time.

A false positive is not a neutral error. Its cost compounds. The first one gets investigated. The tenth gets dismissed. By the fiftieth, people have learned the warning is usually wrong and click through without reading it.

You have not only wasted their time. You have trained them to ignore you, and the training holds when the alert is finally real.

Testers live the same dynamic with flaky tests. A suite failing for no reason two mornings a week is not a slightly worse suite. It is one that no longer changes anybody's behaviour, because red has stopped meaning anything.

Which is why a false positive rate deserves the same seriousness as a miss rate. Both destroy the value of a signal, just at different speeds.

If your alerts were wrong one time in ten, how long before your team stopped reading them?
